problem: Prior zero-shot VLM-based navigators such as CoW and LM-Nav use CLIP only as a critic that matches images to object-goal text. This matching is disjoint from mapping, so they cannot associate multiple views of the same object, cannot localize spatial goals ('in between the sofa and the TV', '3 m right of the chair'), and do not build a persistent representation that different embodiments can share. Classic geometric/semantic maps are spatially precise but limited to closed vocabularies.
motivation: Internet-scale VLMs give open-vocabulary grounding, and geometric maps give spatial precision; the paper asks whether one can have both. Its central observation is that anchoring dense, pixel-aligned VLM (CLIP-space) features onto a 3D reconstruction makes the map itself indexable by natural language. Code-writing LLMs can then compose precise, parameterized spatial navigation calls against that map.
key_idea: Back-project dense LSeg pixel embeddings (in CLIP space) onto a top-down grid map built from RGB-D and odometry, averaging across views, so that landmarks, obstacle classes and spatial goals can be localized by CLIP-text similarity and driven by LLM-generated Python code.
insight: Pixel-level, language-aligned features fused across views give much cleaner object masks than GradCAM saliency (CoW) or projected global CLIP features. This shows most directly in the CLIP Map ablation: the same pipeline with CLIP instead of LSeg features drops multi-object SR@1 from 59 to 33 and SR@4 from 15 to 0. Top-down segmentation confirms it: mIoU 19.0 vs 5.7 for CoW, pixel accuracy 92.3 vs 66.1. Spatial goals amplify localization errors, since the robot must reach an offset relative to the object; with the same code-generation front-end, CoW/CLIP Map collapse to 5/0% at two subgoals in a row while VLMaps reaches 33%. Because obstacle maps come from open-vocabulary queries on a shared map, a drone map that omits furniture keeps success (56 vs 53) while raising SPL (45.4 vs 41.8 at 1 subgoal).
method: VLMap construction: for each RGB-D frame, back-project depth pixels with K^-1 and camera pose T_Wk to world points, then project them to a top-down grid (H̄×W̄, scale s). Each pixel's LSeg visual-encoder embedding (C-dim, CLIP space) is assigned to its grid cell, and all embeddings (across points and frames) falling in a cell are averaged.

Open-vocabulary landmark indexing: encode a user list of category strings with the CLIP text encoder (prompt-template ensemble, e.g. 'A photo of {label}'), compute similarity S = Q·E^T between flattened map features and text embeddings, and take argmax per cell to get a segmentation of the map.

Open-vocabulary obstacle maps: build a height-filtered geometric occupancy map O (points with t1 ≤ y ≤ t2). Take the union of the indexed masks for an embodiment-specific subset of obstacle categories and intersect it with O to drop false positives on the floor. This yields per-embodiment maps (e.g. LoCoBot vs drone) from the same VLMap.

LLM code generation: a code-writing LLM (Codex-style) is few-shot prompted with comment→code pairs. It translates free-form instructions into executable Python calling parameterized primitives (move_to_left, move_in_between, move_north, face, turn, move_forward, get_pos, loops, arithmetic), and the code is run with exec.

Navigation primitives: each primitive localizes the nearest matching landmark in the VLMap, applies a predefined scripted offset for relations such as left/right/north/between, and plans on the embodiment-specific obstacle map with an off-the-shelf navigation stack. Low-level execution uses forward 0.05 m / turn 1° actions.

numbers_note: All evaluations use the paper's own custom benchmarks, not standard ObjectNav/VLN splits; 'split' is set to 'test' only as a placeholder. A 'GT Map' oracle row (ground-truth semantic map, same pipeline) is reported as an upper bound but not listed: multi-object 91/78/71/67/85; spatial 76/48/33/29. Per-class IoU is in an appendix table (e.g., chair 77.04, seating 0.00).
results: On 91 multi-object navigation sequences in Habitat/MP3D, VLMaps reaches 59% SR for 1 subgoal and 15% for 4 in a row, vs the best baseline CoW at 42%/3% (LM-Nav 26/1, CLIP Map 33/0); independent subgoal SR is 59 vs 36. On 21 language-specified spatial-goal trajectories, VLMaps gets 62/33/14/10% vs CoW's 33/5/0/0, using the same LLM code-generation front-end. A drone-specific obstacle map from the same VLMap raises SPL (45.4 vs 41.8 at 1 subgoal) while keeping SR; the real HSR robot completes 10 of 20 spatial goals.
limitations: Sensitive to 3D reconstruction noise, inaccurate depth and odometry drift; the map must be pre-built from an exploration pass over a static scene, with no dynamic objects or humans.

Cannot disambiguate among multiple similar objects in cluttered scenes; per-cell feature averaging adds noise; LSeg misaligns categories outside its training set (e.g., 'seating' gets 0 IoU, and sofa and chair get confused).
Spatial relations come from hand-scripted offsets and primitives, and evaluation uses small custom benchmarks rather than standard VLN/ObjectNav splits.
